title: Ten copies beat one blank page
whisper: Copy it. Compare it. Fix it.
_note: Rendered in raea (raea/ungraded-005-copy); the beats carry the script and the page, cues live in the composition.

beats.say: Ten copies teach you more than one blank page.
Most people think copying is cheating.
And at school, they're right. Copy a friend's homework, and you get a zero.
But out here, the rules flip.
Nobody grades your copies. They only see what you make after them.
Here's a real one. Benjamin Franklin leaves school at ten.
As a young apprentice, he finds a volume of The Spectator, a London paper. He loves the writing, and wants to write like that.
So he makes short notes on each sentence, and puts the book away.
Days later, he rewrites the essays from his notes alone.
Then he compares his copy with the original, finds his faults, and fixes them.
At night, after work. Early in the morning. On Sundays.
His goal? In his own words, to become a "tolerable" English writer.
Later, he writes and prints Poor Richard's Almanack.
Copy someone's work and sign it? Still cheating. Copy to learn? That's practice.
Picture learning to draw. Copy a sketch. Copy it again, from memory. Then change one thing, and sign that.
Ten copies? Ten lessons. A blank page you're scared of? Zero.
So the next time you're stuck, copy something. Because…
